demographics.trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another

vignette:
She is 31 and has built a life around being visible on purpose. As a social media manager, she spends her days shaping other people's images, choosing what is polished, what looks effortless, what can be posted and forgotten. That control used to suit her. After the accident, it feels like a thin membrane stretched over something much more chaotic.

The event happened in a single instant, but in her telling it is split into fragments that keep returning. She was driving on a day that felt ordinary enough to be forgettable. She was thinking about a work deadline, a message from her ex-husband she had not answered, and whether she needed to buy groceries after work. At an intersection, she made a mistake-one she still has trouble naming without her voice tightening. Another vehicle entered her path. The collision was sudden and violent. In the aftermath, she heard screaming and saw that someone had been seriously injured because of what she had done. She describes the moment as if the world did not just break, but tipped into a different version of itself that she cannot leave.

In the weeks that followed, she moved through the formalities with a kind of stunned obedience. She answered police questions, spoke to insurance representatives, and tried to function at work, where she could still schedule posts and answer clients with the practiced confidence that had once come easily. But she says she was no longer actually present. Her body would be at her desk while her mind replayed the sound of impact, the look on the injured person's face, the terrible fact that her mistake had changed someone else's life. She begins to feel contaminated by the event, as though there is something permanently damaged in her that other people can somehow see.

She sleeps poorly. When she does fall asleep, she wakes abruptly, heart pounding, with the same image in her mind: the intersection, the metal crunching, the body thrown off balance. Sometimes she dreams that she is back at the wheel and cannot make her hands work. Other times she dreams she is the injured person, and she wakes with a sharp, animal dread that leaves her shaking in the dark. In the morning, she often lies still for several minutes before getting out of bed, listening for traffic outside and bracing herself against the day ahead.

Driving becomes one of the hardest parts of her life. She first avoids it completely, arranging rides and making excuses, then later forces herself to drive only short distances with her hands locked tightly on the steering wheel. At intersections she freezes, checking and rechecking, her pulse racing so fast that she sometimes has to pull over. She avoids the route where the accident happened, even though it makes her commute longer and more complicated. She notices she is always scanning for danger now, interpreting sudden sounds as threats, flinching at horns, and tensing when someone brakes too quickly in front of her.

At work, she remains competent in a way that surprises people who do not know her well. She still manages campaigns, writes captions, and monitors analytics, but the work takes more effort than it used to. She rereads messages repeatedly, afraid of making another irreversible mistake. A part of her feels she does not deserve the ease of ordinary tasks. She becomes irritable when colleagues complain about minor problems, then feels ashamed for being cold. Some days she tears up unexpectedly while reviewing content, especially if an ad involves cars, roads, or any image of speed. She quickly closes the screen and tells herself to keep going.

Her divorce has become tangled with the trauma in ways she is only beginning to understand. The marriage ended before the accident, but since then she feels even more isolated, as if she has lost the ability to imagine being safely known by another person. She keeps her distance from friends and family, not wanting to hear reassurance she cannot absorb. She worries that if she speaks too honestly, people will see her not as someone who made a mistake, but as the mistake itself. She carries intense guilt, not only about the injured stranger, but about her own survival and the fact that her life has continued.

Over time, she has become more cautious, more guarded, and more exhausted. She still shows up, still posts, still answers messages, but everything is filtered through the accident. She lives with a persistent sense that danger can arrive in an instant, that one decision can split a life open, and that the version of herself who existed before that intersection is somewhere behind her, unreachable.
